rows: Acrylamide can form naturally when starchy foods are cooked at high temperatures.
It is not deliberately added to food.
Food businesses must use appropriate acrylamide mitigation measures within their food-safety management systems.
Cooking methods, time, temperature, recipe and raw materials influence acrylamide formation.
Businesses should avoid unnecessary over-browning while still cooking food safely.
Manufacturer cooking instructions should be followed for relevant products.
Benchmark levels support monitoring and investigation rather than acting as simple legal maximums for every sample.
FSA surveys and targeted investigations monitor acrylamide in foods and the effectiveness of controls.
A food category or dark colour alone does not establish the acrylamide concentration of a specific item.
Product-level conclusions require validated sampling, laboratory analysis and process information.
Campylobacter is a common cause of food poisoning and raw poultry is an important source.
Raw chicken should be covered and stored at the bottom of the refrigerator so juices cannot drip onto other foods.
Raw chicken should not be washed because splashing can spread bacteria.
Chicken and other poultry must be cooked thoroughly according to safe time and temperature guidance.
Hands, utensils and work surfaces should be cleaned after contact with raw poultry.
Raw poultry must be kept separate from ready-to-eat food.
Slaughterhouse and retail monitoring programmes measure Campylobacter contamination and support control action.
Food businesses should apply food-safety management, hygiene and staff-training controls across the chain.
A poultry product or premises type does not prove that a particular batch contains Campylobacter.
Product attribution requires batch, sampling, laboratory, handling and epidemiological evidence.
Raw drinking milk has not been heat-treated to destroy harmful microorganisms.
FSA guidance requires producers to use an effective and verified food-safety management system.
Controls include animal health, milking hygiene, equipment cleanliness, storage and microbiological testing.
Raw milk must be handled and kept chilled to limit microbial growth.
Required consumer warnings communicate that raw milk may contain harmful organisms.
Children, pregnant people, older people and those with weakened immunity are at greater risk from foodborne infection.
Producers and sellers must comply with the applicable registration, sales and labelling controls.
Pasteurisation substantially reduces microbiological risks associated with milk.
Raw-milk status does not prove that a particular batch is contaminated.
Batch-level safety requires current producer, temperature, hygiene, sampling and laboratory evidence.
Shellfish businesses are subject to official controls, production-area classification and approval requirements.
Official programmes monitor phytoplankton and marine biotoxins in shellfish production areas.
Chemical-contaminant monitoring and production-area assessments support harvest controls.
Supplementary sampling can be used when monitoring indicates increased or uncertain risk.
Raw-oyster norovirus incidents require specific investigation and management.
Validated chemical methods support official analysis of regulated shellfish toxins.
Authorities can restrict harvesting or place product controls when monitoring thresholds or incident evidence require action.
Traceability is necessary to link harvested shellfish to production areas, dates and businesses.
Production-area results do not prove that every individual shellfish has the same toxin or pathogen level.
For some emerging marine biotoxins, evidence is insufficient to derive health-based guidance values, so uncertainty must be retained.
